The first, over how much higher interest rates need to go, gets settled at policy meetings. The second, over how much to tell the public about where rates could be headed, is playing out in the open.

   Chairman Kevin Warsh has made a point of saying less. Most of his colleagues haven’t followed his lead. 

   The 16 Fed officials who have been in their posts at least a year gave no less than 59 speeches, interviews and other public comments between last month’s meeting and the quiet period ahead of this week’s gathering, according to a Wall Street Journal tally. That is about equal to the roughly 54 they gave in the same stretch a year earlier. Warsh became Fed chair in May.

   “It doesn’t seem like he’s convinced the others to speak less,” said Kathy Bostjancic, chief economist at Nationwide. “If Warsh doesn’t speak, others fill the void.”

   Below, some of the best analysis and insight from WSJ writers and columnists, the Dow Jones Newswires team and occasionally beyond, on investing, the wealth-management business and more.

       Planning & Investing   The ‘Buy, Borrow and Die’ Wealth Strategy Has Become a $5 Trillion Market   Deloitte study finds booming market in stock-based loans to billionaires— and the lesser rich. 

       Market Talk   From Dow Jones Newswires 

   Insurers are upping their investments in private markets funds, according to a BlackRock survey of 463 insurers across 31 markets. More than two-fifths of global insurers now allocate over 15% of their investment portfolios to private markets, the survey says. Around three-quarters of those surveyed plan to increase their investments in the asset class over the next 12 months. “Over the past decade, private markets have evolved from an alternative source of yield into an established component of portfolios,” BlackRock strategists say. Private debt is particularly in focus, with 41% of respondents saying the area is a target for increased investment. (josephmichael.stonor@wsj.com)

   The government is trying to balance spending and fiscal discipline with its plan to give around 20 billion pounds to the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank, Morgan Stanley says. “The government is seeking to boost investment while not breaching fiscal rules,” Morgan Stanley’s Bruna Skarica says in a note. Both institutions aim to provide financing for economic development in strategic sectors. Should the funds be issued to the private sector as loans, these would be viewed as financial assets for the public sector, netting off the financial liability from increased government borrowing, Skarica says. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

Federal Reserve officials are having two debates at once this fall. The first, over how much higher interest rates need to go, gets settled at policy meetings. The second, over how much to tell the public about where rates could be headed, is playing out in the open.

 

Chairman Kevin Warsh has made a point of saying less. Most of his colleagues haven’t followed his lead.

That is about equal to the roughly 54 they gave in the same stretch a year earlier. Warsh became Fed chair in May.

From Dow Jones Newswires

 

Insurers are upping their investments in private markets funds, according to a BlackRock survey of 463 insurers across 31 markets. Private debt is particularly in focus, with 41% of respondents saying the area is a target for increased investment. (josephmichael.stonor@wsj.com)

 

The government is trying to balance spending and fiscal discipline with its plan to give around 20 billion pounds to the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank, Morgan Stanley says. “The government is seeking to boost investment while not breaching fiscal rules,” Morgan Stanley’s Bruna Skarica says in a note. Both institutions aim to provide financing for economic development in strategic sectors. Should the funds be issued to the private sector as loans, these would be viewed as financial assets for the public sector, netting off the financial liability from increased government borrowing, Skarica says.
